title: Computing history
blurb: Clever machines and the people who taught them to think in numbers.

notes.abacus: Beads on rods: people have done sums this way for thousands of years.
notes.algorithm: A step-by-step recipe for solving a problem, named after the Persian scholar al-Khwarizmi.
notes.analog: Analog computers solved problems with smoothly changing voltages or turning wheels instead of digits.
notes.arcade: Arcade cabinets of the 1970s took video games out of university labs and into everyday places.
notes.array: A row of values stored side by side, each one found by its position number.
notes.assembler: A program that turns short, readable instructions into the raw numbers a processor runs.
notes.automaton: A self-moving machine; clockwork automatons that could write and draw were built in the 1700s.
notes.avatar: A picture or character that stands for you in a game or an online space.
notes.backspace: The key that rubs out the letter behind the cursor; on typewriters it simply stepped back one space.
notes.backup: A spare copy of your files, kept safe in case the original gets lost or broken.
notes.bandwidth: How much data a connection can carry each second, a bit like the width of a water pipe.
notes.basic: A friendly programming language from 1964, made so that students could write programs easily.
notes.baud: A measure of signal changes per second, named after the telegraph inventor Emile Baudot.
notes.binary: Counting with only two digits, 0 and 1, which is how computers store everything.
notes.boot: Short for bootstrap: a tiny starter program loads a bigger one, which loads the rest.
notes.bootstrap: Starting a computer is called booting, from the old idea of pulling yourself up by your bootstraps.
notes.broadband: A fast, always-on internet link that replaced slow dial-up modems in many homes in the 2000s.
notes.browser: A program for visiting web pages; Tim Berners-Lee wrote the very first one in 1990.
notes.buffer: A small waiting area in memory where data sits until the computer is ready for it.
notes.byte: A group of eight bits, enough to store one letter of plain English text.
notes.cache: A fast little store of recently used things, so the computer need not fetch them again.
notes.calculator: Pocket electronic calculators appeared in the early 1970s and soon replaced slide rules.
notes.cartridge: Plug-in game cartridges kept their programs on chips, so games started almost instantly.
notes.cassette: Many home computers of the early 1980s loaded their programs from ordinary audio tapes.
notes.cipher: A secret way of scrambling a message so that only someone with the key can read it.
notes.circuit: A closed loop that electricity flows around; computers are built from vast numbers of them.
notes.client: In client and server computing the client asks and the server answers; the web works this way.
notes.colossus: Built in Britain in 1944, Colossus was one of the first programmable electronic computers.
notes.command: Before windows and icons, people typed commands to tell a computer what to do next.
notes.compiler: A program that translates code people write into instructions a machine can run.
notes.compression: Squeezing data into less space by spotting patterns and writing them more briefly.
notes.computer: Once a job title: computers were people who worked out long calculations by hand.
notes.console: Early computers were run from a console: a desk of switches, dials and blinking lamps.
notes.crash: A sudden stop. Early disk drives could crash for real, their heads striking the spinning disk.
notes.cryptography: The science of secret codes drove the building of some of the very first computers.
notes.cursor: The blinking marker that shows where your next letter will appear on the screen.
notes.cybernetics: The study of control and feedback in machines and living things, named by Norbert Wiener in 1948.
notes.cyberspace: A word made up by science fiction writer William Gibson in the early 1980s for the online world.
notes.database: A tidy store of information that a program can search and sort quickly.
notes.debugger: A tool for finding mistakes in programs by running them one small step at a time.
notes.decimal: Counting in tens; some early computers, such as ENIAC, worked in decimal rather than binary.
notes.desktop: The on-screen workspace of icons and windows, named after a real desk.
notes.digital: Working with whole numbers, like counting on fingers, instead of smoothly changing values.
notes.directory: A folder that holds files and other folders, arranged like the branches of a tree.
notes.diskette: Another name for the floppy disk, the bendy square that carried files between computers.
notes.domain: The readable name of a website, so people need not remember a long string of numbers.
notes.download: Copying a file from another computer, usually over the internet, onto your own.
notes.electronic: The first electronic computers of the 1940s switched with vacuum tubes instead of moving parts.
notes.email: Messages between computers began in the 1960s; the @ sign was first used for email in 1971.
notes.emulator: A program that pretends to be another machine, so old software can run on new computers.
notes.encryption: Scrambling data so that only someone with the right key can unscramble and read it.
notes.enigma: Enigma was a German wartime cipher machine; codebreakers built special machines to read its messages.
notes.firewall: A guard program that decides which network traffic may come in or go out.
notes.firmware: Software built into a device's memory chips that starts it up and keeps it working.
notes.floppy: Flexible disks first sold in the early 1970s; for years they were how people shared files.
notes.folder: Folders on screen borrowed their name and picture from the paper folders of an office.
notes.font: A complete set of letters in one style; computers let anyone switch fonts with a click.
notes.function: A named set of instructions that takes some inputs and hands back a result.
notes.gate: A logic gate combines bits: AND, OR and NOT gates built from transistors make up every chip.
notes.gigabyte: About a billion bytes: enough room for hundreds of songs.
notes.gigahertz: Home computer processors passed one gigahertz, a billion clock ticks a second, in 2000.
notes.glitch: A small, unexpected fault that makes a program or picture behave oddly for a moment.
notes.graphics: Pictures made by computers; many early screens could draw only glowing lines and letters.
notes.hacker: Hacker first meant a playful, clever programmer, a word from student clubs of the late 1950s.
notes.hamming: Richard Hamming invented codes in 1950 that let computers spot and fix their own small errors.
notes.hardware: The parts of a computer you can touch, as opposed to the programs that run on it.
notes.hexadecimal: Counting in sixteens with the digits 0 to 9 and A to F, a neat shorthand for binary.
notes.hobbyist: Hobbyists of the 1970s built home computers from kits and swapped programs at club meetings.
notes.hopper: Grace Hopper, a pioneering programmer, helped make computer languages read more like English.
notes.hyperlink: Clickable text or pictures that jump you to another page.
notes.hypertext: Text with links to other text; Ted Nelson came up with the word in the 1960s.
notes.icon: A tiny picture you click to open a program or file instead of typing a command.
notes.integer: A whole number with no fraction, one of the first kinds of value computers handled.
notes.interpreter: Runs a program line by line, which made the languages of home computers quick to try out.
notes.joystick: A stick you tilt to steer; aircraft pilots used them long before home video games did.
notes.kernel: The heart of an operating system, which shares out memory and time among programs.
notes.keyboard: Computer keyboards borrowed their letter layout from typewriters of the 1870s.
notes.keypunch: Programmers typed their code onto cards with a keypunch, one card for every line.
notes.kilobyte: About a thousand bytes; many early home computers had only a few kilobytes of memory.
notes.laptop: A computer that folds up and rests on your lap; the first ones appeared in the early 1980s.
notes.lisp: One of the oldest programming languages still in use, created by John McCarthy in 1958.
notes.logarithm: Logarithms, published in 1614, turned long multiplication into simple addition.
notes.logbook: In 1947 a moth found inside a Harvard computer was taped into its logbook as an actual bug.
notes.logic: George Boole's logic of true and false, published in 1854, became the rules every circuit follows.
notes.logo: A 1967 teaching language in which children steer a little turtle around to draw pictures.
notes.loom: From 1804 a weaving loom followed patterns punched into chains of cards, an idea computers borrowed.
notes.loop: Repeats steps until a condition is met, so a short program can do a great deal of work.
notes.macro: Records a run of keystrokes or commands so that one key can replay them all.
notes.mainframe: A big, powerful computer shared by many users, often filling a whole room in the 1960s.
notes.megabyte: About a million bytes; a floppy disk of the 1990s held about one and a half of them.
notes.memory: Core memory of the 1950s stored each bit in a tiny magnetic ring threaded on crossed wires.
notes.microchip: A tiny slice of silicon packed with circuits; the first chips were made in 1958 and 1959.
notes.minicomputer: Smaller and cheaper than a mainframe, minicomputers of the 1960s let labs own their own machine.
notes.modem: Short for modulator-demodulator: it turned data into sounds that could travel down a phone line.
notes.monitor: The screen that shows what a computer is doing; early ones glowed green or amber on black.
notes.motherboard: The main circuit board that every other part of a computer plugs into.
notes.mouse: Douglas Engelbart's team built the first computer mouse in the 1960s, carved from wood.
notes.multimedia: Mixing text, sound, pictures and video in one program, a big idea of the early 1990s.
notes.nanosecond: A billionth of a second; Grace Hopper handed out foot-long wires to show how far light goes in one.
notes.network: Computers joined together so they can share files, messages and printers.
notes.nibble: Half a byte, or four bits: a little joke by programmers on the word bite.
notes.numeral: Hindu-Arabic numerals, with a zero, made written arithmetic far easier than Roman numerals.
notes.octal: Writing numbers in base eight; machines with 12-, 18- or 36-bit words often showed them that way.
notes.online: Connected to a network, so you can reach other computers and the people using them.
notes.operator: Early computers needed operators who loaded tapes and cards and watched the blinking lights.
notes.oscilloscope: An instrument that draws electric signals as wavy lines; one of the first video games ran on one.
notes.packet: A small bundle of data; the internet splits messages into packets and joins them up again at the end.
notes.pager: Pagers beeped to ask people to call someone back; later models showed short text messages.
notes.password: A secret word that proves who you are; shared computers began asking for them in the early 1960s.
notes.phosphor: The glowing coating inside old screens that lit up wherever a beam of electrons struck it.
notes.pixel: Short for picture element: one of the tiny dots that make up a screen image.
notes.plotter: A machine that drew diagrams with real pens moving across paper, guided by a computer.
notes.pointer: A value that holds the address of something else in memory, like a signpost.
notes.printer: Line printers hammered out a whole line of text at a time, hundreds of lines a minute.
notes.processor: The part of a computer that follows instructions; a whole processor first fit on one chip in 1971.
notes.program: A list of instructions for a computer; Ada Lovelace wrote one of the very first, on paper.
notes.programmer: Many of the first programmers were women, including the six who programmed ENIAC.
notes.prompt: The mark a computer shows when it is ready for your next typed command.
notes.protocol: An agreed set of rules that lets two computers understand each other's messages.
notes.punched: Punched cards stored data as holes; the American census of 1890 was counted with them.
notes.radar: Wartime radar work gave early computers fast pulse circuits and their first memory tubes.
notes.raster: A raster screen draws its picture as rows of dots, like a television, instead of tracing lines.
notes.recursion: When a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem.
notes.robot: The word comes from a Czech play of 1920; real machines took the name decades later.
notes.robotics: The science of robots; science fiction writer Isaac Asimov was the first to use the word, in 1941.
notes.router: A box that passes data between networks, choosing a route for every packet.
notes.scanner: A machine that turns paper pictures into pixels; the first scanned photo, in 1957, showed a baby.
notes.server: A computer that hands out files or pages to other computers that ask for them.
notes.silicon: The element found in sand that most computer chips are made from.
notes.simulator: The Whirlwind computer began in the 1940s as part of a project to build a flight simulator.
notes.software: The programs a computer runs, as opposed to the hardware you can touch.
notes.sorting: Card sorters put punched cards in order decades before sorting became a classic programming task.
notes.spool: Spooling lines up jobs for a slow device such as a printer, so the computer need not wait.
notes.spreadsheet: A grid of cells that does sums for you; the first one for personal computers came out in 1979.
notes.sprite: A small picture that moves around a game screen, like a character or a ball.
notes.storage: Keeps data while the power is off: punched cards first, then tape, disks and finally chips.
notes.stylus: A pen-shaped pointer for a screen; light pens did the same job back in the 1950s.
notes.subroutine: A small, reusable piece of a program that can be called on whenever it is needed.
notes.syntax: The grammar rules of a programming language; one misplaced symbol can stop a program.
notes.tablet: Long before touch screens, a 1964 graphics tablet let people draw into a computer with a pen.
notes.tabulator: Punched-card machines that counted and sorted data, decades before electronic computers.
notes.tally: Tally marks scratched on bones and sticks are among the oldest known ways of keeping count.
notes.tape: Magnetic tape stored data on long reels that whirred back and forth to find a record.
notes.telegraph: The electric telegraph of the 1830s sent messages as pulses down a wire, a forerunner of networks.
notes.terabyte: About a million megabytes; the first one-terabyte hard drive went on sale in 2007.
notes.terminal: A keyboard and screen linked to a distant computer, often shared by many people.
notes.transistor: A tiny electric switch invented in 1947 that replaced bulky, hot vacuum tubes.
notes.typewriter: Typewriters gave computers their keyboard layout and the idea of a carriage return.
notes.valve: In Britain vacuum tubes were called valves; thousands of them glowed inside each early computer.
notes.variable: A named box in a program that holds a value, which can change as the program runs.
notes.vector: Graphics drawn from lines and curves instead of dots, so they stay sharp at any size.
notes.virus: A program that copies itself onto other computers, named after the germs that spread illness.
notes.wafer: Chips are made many at a time on a thin round wafer of silicon, then cut apart.
notes.website: The very first website, which explained the web itself, went public in 1991.
notes.window: A framed area on the screen showing one program, so several can be open at once.
notes.wireless: Wireless networking let computers join a network without a cable; it spread through homes in the 2000s.
notes.worm: A program that copies itself from computer to computer; one released in 1988 slowed thousands of machines.
